captures.transcript:
“I remember another life. Approximately forty years. Nineteen to fifty-nine.”

Nothing happened.

I had expected that sentence to feel larger.

It did not.

It sounded exactly like what it was.

A man in a cave saying something impossible.

“The childhood before that was the same. Or close enough that I never found a difference worth keeping. I did not return to birth. I woke at nineteen.”

His eye moved over my face.

Then lower.

The ruined leg.

I opened my mouth.

Closed it.

I hated that he was already getting better at this.

“Years.”

The eye narrowed.

“There were little things early. People saying something differently. A shop closing on the wrong month. Weather. I ignored most of it because people remember weather badly and shops close whenever they feel like failing.”

The larger things came later.

Years later.

That sounded bad when I said it out loud.

The pupil tightened again.

I had managed to surprise a dragon twice in one morning.

It was not improving my odds of leaving.

“How she got trapped is a long story.”

His chin settled onto the stone.

Not bored this time.

Comfortable.

That was worse.

He was becoming pleased with the existence of long stories.

“In that history she told me your name. She also told me how to cross the mountain.”

Ithar's eye moved to my coat.

The sulfur residue.

The clean boots.

It was not really a seat.

It was a part of the cave that happened to be roughly the right height and only moderately covered in old coins.

My left leg preferred sitting to standing.

The rest of me had not yet decided whether sitting in a dragon's home counted as progress.

“The Line is failing now. That part has a clock. You still haven't agreed to help, so I should probably keep saying it.”

Ithar's claw moved through the gold again.

The sound was becoming background noise.

captures.transcript:
The cave suddenly felt warmer.

“Don't.”

His eye remained on me.

I waited.

He waited longer.

I hated him a little.

The claw dragged a shallow line through the gold.

Coins rolled into it and vanished.

He wanted the end of the first life.

I could feel the question coming without hearing it spoken.

“No.”

The pupil shifted.

“We're not doing this. We're discussing the Line.”

As far as Ithar was concerned, we had finished discussing the Line when he refused to promise anything.

I regretted several answers I had not even said out loud.

“I can hunt.”

His eye dropped to the leg.

“Poorly.”

That one I admitted for him.

The word perhaps sat between us without being spoken.

I had come here to save the Line.

Perhaps.

I looked at the passage again.

The exit did not help.

“What if I say no?”

The dragon answered without ceremony.

“You leave. You may die on the mountain. You may live. The Line may fail. I will not burn you for refusing conversation.”

Memory gets cleaned when you use it too often. It keeps the line and loses the breath before it. The scrape in the throat. The way she said quieter like I had personally offended the concept.

This had all of it.

I sat there until she kicked the wall once and went away.

Then I got out of bed.

My feet hit cold boards.

Both knees bent.

Nothing hurt.

That almost put me back down.

I had been nineteen once already.

I remembered thinking I was strong for nineteen.

“He's nineteen. Maybe hands are interesting now.”

“Fuck you,” I said.

My mother pointed the spoon at me.

“Greg.”

“Sorry.”

My father lowered the sheet.

For one second I saw the old man he never got to become.

Then it was gone.

He was forty-three and trying not to smile.

I sat down.

My sister came in wearing one boot and carrying the other.

“You look weird.”

“Thank you.”

“No. Like actually.”

“I slept bad.”

“You were punching your bed.”

“I was testing something.”

captures.transcript:
He looked at me strangely.

“You feeling all right?”

“Everyone keeps asking me that.”

“Because you're acting like somebody hit you in the head.”

“Maybe somebody did.”

My sister took my last piece of bread.

I let her.

That scared her more than anything else.

“What?” I asked.

She stared at the bread in her hand.

“You didn't fight me.”

“I can take another piece.”

“You always fight me.”

“Maybe I've grown.”

“You look the same.”

I laughed.

She did not know why.

Neither did I, really.

I knew how to fix that.

That was the dangerous part.

I knew reinforcement better than most instructors who had ever taught me. I knew breathing sequences. Load paths. How to move pressure through the hips without wasting it in the spine. How to hold a sheath under the skin and let impact disperse instead of stopping it.

The knowledge was there.

My body was nineteen.

I smiled.

Then I did something stupid.

Not very stupid.

I had standards by then.

For a few minutes it did.

I could rebuild faster.

Smarter.

Skip the broken wrist.

Skip Kett.

Skip the winter fever.

Skip all the expensive lessons and arrive at the same summit with fewer scars.

That was the first plan.

It was a good plan.

I had been very good at plans by the end of my first life.

The doors opened.

People moved around me.

I crossed the street.

The first time it had taken me almost two hours.

That felt good for about three questions.

Then I hit the practical section.

A brass plate sat on the table with six carved channels, two pressure points, and one cracked retention ring.

The examiner was a narrow man with gray hair tied behind his head.

“Identify the unsafe load path.”

I looked at the plate.

I knew three better ways to build the thing.

I knew how it failed under field pressure.

It was.

Some things survived history.

“Contract board is through there,” Mira said.

“I know.”

She looked at me.

I pointed vaguely.

“Sign.”

There was a sign.

“Mm.”

I left before I created a new history where Mira disliked me nineteen years earlier than scheduled.

The contract board occupied an entire wall.

Wooden rails. Paper slips. Wax tags for urgency. Colored corners for hazard class.

I had never asked who did.

The Line had been something under the world that behaved until it didn't.

At fifty-nine, I knew the western system was failing because people had forgotten what sat below the surface works.

At nineteen, a contract offered eight silver a week to scrape rust off part of it.

I took the slip.

The clerk at the assignment desk looked at my temporary badge, then at me.

“You have maintenance experience?”

“Yes.”

He looked down at the form.

“No certification.”

That was what had been inside.

I stopped in the doorway.

She looked up.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You got work?”

“Yeah.”

“When do you leave?”

“I don't.”

She frowned.

“What?”

“East Four. Starts tomorrow.”

“Oh.”

She went back to tying wire through one of the lantern frames.

Then, like it did not matter, she said, “So you're helping Saturday.”

I looked at the green box.

“Yeah.”

She nodded once.

No gratitude.

No dramatic reconciliation with a brother she had never lost.

“At the time it felt temporary.”

His eye held mine.

I closed my eyes again.

I believed the paper too.

People I had only known as names, supervisors, officers, legends, or corpses turned out to be ordinary sizes when I met them before the story I remembered attached itself.

Dera had iron-gray hair even then and arms like somebody had built them for carrying pipe.

She looked at the six of us.

Then at our boots.

Then back at us.

“Anyone wearing a ring?”

Two people checked their hands.

“Take them off.”

One man asked why.

Dera pointed at a black mark halfway up the nearest wall.

Dera put me on the weekend crew because I could hear a bad bearing before most of the older hands.

Nessa learned I knew more than my badge said and started asking questions when nobody else was listening.

My father needed help replacing a mill shaft.

My sister got work at a printer and developed the expensive habit of bringing home paper she claimed had been thrown away.

My field evaluations were high enough for formal Ranker testing.

I left it on the kitchen table for three days.

captures.transcript:
The first future I changed on purpose belonged to three men I had never met.

That sounds important now.

At the time it was paperwork.

East Four received a bypass order in the fifth year.

New upper feed from Market Two. Revised load allocation. Temporary closure of the south channel while the tram authority replaced stone above it.

The kind of project that arrived in a rolled plan tube and immediately created six arguments about whose problem it was.

I was twenty-four.

D-class by then.

Still working maintenance.

Still going home most nights.

Still training enough that I could pretend I had not stopped climbing.

Halden stood over a plan for North Three and asked, “What do you see?”

I looked.

“Bad drainage.”

“What else?”

“Old foundation under the west wall.”

“What else?”

I looked at him.

“You already found the problem.”

“Yes.”

“Then why am I here?”

“To see if you do.”

“That is rude.”

“Yes.”

“You're going to need another one.”

“I think something fails during transfer.”

“You think.”

“Yes.”

“Based on?”

I looked out across the roofs.

At twenty-six in my first life, I had been in another province killing something with too many legs.

I knew the accident happened.

I knew who died.

I knew almost nothing about why.

The report had blamed a transfer fault.

Later reporting blamed maintenance.

“I knew something.”

“What?”

“That the transfer went bad.”

“How?”

The cave went quiet.

I was under the upper manifold with both arms inside a housing when somebody entered the chamber behind me.

Heavy boots.

Measured pace.

No limp.

Dera said, “You're early.”

A man answered, “The road was dry.”

My hand stopped inside the machine.

The voice was younger than the one in my memory.

Of course it was.

So was mine.

I pulled my arms free and hit my elbow on the housing.

“Fuck.”

Nessa looked over from the pressure desk.

“You all right?”

“No.”

That got her attention.

Halden joined a central review.

The review corrected North Vey.

North Vey never ruptured.

Bren never broke his ankle.

Never got the scar.

Still became A-class through some road I did not know.

The future had not merely changed.

It had begun replacing itself.

“What's funny?” Bren asked.

“Nothing.”

“That didn't look like nothing.”

“Long story.”

He nodded toward the bulletin.

“You know Halden?”

“Yes.”

“Good?”

“Annoying.”

“Usually means good.”

“Unfortunately.”

Bren smiled.

“He didn't owe me the man I remembered.”
